title: Caching Basics
subtitle: Watch one hot record get read and written through a cache, and see how each policy trades speed, freshness, and safety.
learn: How cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-back, and write-around differ
How hit ratio turns into average latency and database load
How LRU and LFU choose what to throw out when the cache is full
Where caches live between the browser and the database

steps.title: The same row, ten thousand times
steps.body: Imagine a product page that keeps asking for the same few popular rows. Say 10,000 reads arrive every second, and each database read takes about 10 ms. With no cache, the database answers all 10,000 every second, even though most answers are identical repeats. A cache is a small, fast store (usually in memory) that remembers answers so the database does not repeat the work. We assume a cache read takes about 1 ms.
steps.idea: A cache spends a little memory, and risks slightly old data, to avoid many slow repeated reads.
steps.caption: No cache yet: every read goes to the database.

steps.title: Cache-aside: the app does the work
steps.body: Cache-aside (also called lazy loading) means the app does the work itself. It asks the cache first. On a miss, meaning the cache does not have the answer, the app reads the database and then saves the result in the cache with a time limit (TTL, time to live) of 300 seconds. This first read costs about 11 ms, because it pays for both the cache check and the database read. Later reads of the same key can use the saved copy.
steps.idea: In cache-aside the app fills the cache on demand, so only data that is really read gets cached.
steps.caption: Miss: the app asks the cache, falls back to the database, then fills the cache.

steps.title: A hit, and why the ratio matters
steps.body: Now the same key is requested again. The cache has it, so this is a hit: the answer returns in about 1 ms and the database does no work. Hit ratio is hits divided by total reads. At 90%, with 1 ms hits and 11 ms misses, average latency is 0.9 x 1 + 0.1 x 11 = 2 ms. Only the 10% of reads that miss reach the database, so it sees 1,000 reads per second instead of 10,000. Going from 90% to 99% cuts that by another 10 times, to 100 per second.
steps.idea: Misses are what you pay for, so even a small hit-ratio gain near the top removes a lot of database load.
steps.caption: Hit: answered from the cache, the database is not touched.

steps.title: Read-through: the cache loads itself
steps.body: Read-through hides the miss logic from the app. The app only ever talks to the cache. If the key is missing, the cache itself fetches it from the database, saves it, and returns it. The result is the same as cache-aside, but the loading code lives in one place (the cache layer or a library) instead of in every caller. Plain Redis does not do this by itself; a library or caching layer in front of it does the loading.
steps.idea: Read-through and cache-aside differ only in who loads on a miss: the cache or the application.
steps.caption: On a miss, the cache (not the app) fetches from the database.

steps.title: Write-through: update both, then confirm
steps.body: Now writes. In write-through, the app sends the update to the cache, which writes it to the database too, and the app hears 'ok' only after both succeed. So cached data always matches saved data, and a cache crash loses nothing. If the database write fails, the cache update must fail or be undone as well. The price: every write waits for the slower database, and you may cache values nobody reads again.
steps.idea: Write-through keeps cache and database in step, but each write is only as fast as the database.
steps.caption: The database confirms the write before the app hears 'ok'.

steps.title: Write-back: acknowledge now, save later
steps.body: Write-back (also called write-behind) is the opposite bet. The cache saves the write, answers 'ok' right away, and copies it to the database later in batches. Entries changed in the cache but not yet saved are called dirty. Writes become very fast, and many updates to one key can collapse into a single database write. The danger: if the cache dies before a flush, those acknowledged writes are lost, unless the cache persists or replicates them.
steps.idea: Write-back is the fastest write path, and the only one that can lose data you already acknowledged.
steps.caption: The cache says 'ok' fast; the worker saves to the database later.

steps.title: Write-around: skip the cache on writes
steps.body: Write-around sends writes straight to the database and skips the cache. It suits data that is written once and rarely read soon after, such as uploaded logs or a bulk import, because it keeps that data from filling the cache. The catch: the first read after a write is a miss, and any older cached copy of that key stays stale until it expires or is removed.
steps.idea: Write-around protects the cache from write-heavy, rarely read data, at the cost of a cold first read.
steps.caption: The write goes to the database only; the cache is untouched.

steps.title: The cache is full: who goes?
steps.body: Memory is limited, so a full cache must evict (throw out) something to make room for a new key. LRU (least recently used) removes the key untouched for the longest time, betting that recent use predicts future use. LFU (least frequently used) removes the key with the fewest accesses, which protects long-term favorites. LRU is simple and common (Redis offers it as allkeys-lru, but you must turn it on), yet a one-time bulk scan can push hot keys out. LFU resists that, but once-popular keys can linger unless counts decay.
steps.idea: Eviction is a bet about the future: LRU bets on recency, LFU bets on popularity.
steps.caption: The cache is full, so storing a new key throws out an old one.

steps.title: Caches live in layers
steps.body: A request can be answered at several layers. The browser caches files and responses. A CDN (content delivery network) edge serves popular content from a server near the user, and on a miss forwards to the app (its origin). The app may keep a small in-process cache, a shared cache such as Redis (an in-memory key-value store) serves all app servers, and the database keeps hot pages in its own memory. Here the logo is answered by the CDN and the user data by the shared cache, so the database is never reached. Closer to the user is faster, but harder to keep fresh.
steps.idea: Put each cache as close to the user as the data's freshness rules allow.
steps.caption: Logo: CDN hit. User data: shared-cache hit. The database is never reached.

steps.title: Pick the policy by the data
steps.body: Reads: cache-aside keeps the loading logic in the app; read-through moves it into the cache. Writes: write-through is safe but slower, write-back is fast but risky, and write-around keeps write-only data out of the cache. Watch hit ratio, because it sets both latency and database load, and choose an eviction policy that fits how your data is accessed. Common pairings: read-through with write-through, or cache-aside where writes go to the database and then delete the cached key. Keeping cached copies correct over time is the next lesson, on invalidation.
steps.idea: Choose read and write policies per data type, then watch the hit ratio.
steps.caption: Five policies, one goal: fewer slow reads.

quiz.q: Cache hits take 1 ms and misses take 11 ms (cache check plus database read). With an 80% hit ratio, what is the average read latency?
quiz.why: Average = 0.8 x 1 + 0.2 x 11 = 0.8 + 2.2 = 3 ms. Only 20% of reads are misses, but they cost 11x a hit, so they supply 2.2 of the 3 ms.

quiz.q: A counter service acknowledges each increment from the cache and flushes to the database every few seconds. The cache server crashes. What is the realistic loss?
options: Nothing, the database always has every write first
The increments not yet flushed, even though they were acknowledged
quiz.why: This is write-back. Unflushed dirty entries live only in the cache, so a crash loses writes the client was told succeeded.

quiz.q: A nightly report reads 5 million rows exactly once, alongside normal traffic. Which cache behavior is most at risk?
options: LRU, because the scan makes one-time keys look recently used and pushes hot keys out
LFU, because scan keys get high counts and push out hot keys
Cache-aside TTL, because scans shorten the TTL
None, since eviction ignores access order
quiz.why: LRU treats every just-read key as valuable, so a big scan evicts the genuinely popular keys. LFU keeps frequently used keys and resists this.

quiz.q: Which data is the best fit for write-around?
options: A user's shopping cart read on every page
A feature flag read by every request
A session token checked on each call
Audit log rows that are written constantly and rarely read back
quiz.why: Write-around avoids filling the cache with data unlikely to be read soon. The cart, flag, and session are read-heavy and belong in the cache.

cheatsheet.def: App checks the cache, on a miss reads the database and fills the cache itself. Most common pattern; only requested data gets cached.
App talks only to the cache; the cache loads missing keys from the database. Same effect as cache-aside, loading logic lives in the cache layer.
Write goes to cache and database together before the ack. Consistent and durable, but writes are as slow as the database.
Write updates only the cache and flushes to the database later. Fastest writes, but unflushed data is lost if the cache fails.
Write goes straight to the database, skipping the cache. Good for write-once, rarely read data; first read afterward is a miss.
Hits divided by total reads. Average latency = hit% x hit time + miss% x miss time; database load = misses per second.
LRU evicts the least recently used key; LFU evicts the least frequently used. LRU is simple but vulnerable to scans; LFU protects steady favorites.
